e.meaning: belonging to Cassius, a Roman family name
e.etymology: From Latin Cassianus, a derivative of the Roman family name Cassius, borne by several early saints. Cassian Andor of the Star Wars series Andor and the film Rogue One renewed it.

assoc.t: Cassian Andor, rebel spy in Star Wars: Andor
Cassian, warrior in A Court of Thorns and Roses

e.etymology: From a French surname, from the Germanic name Landric: land plus ric, mighty ruler. In the US it is tied to Louisiana and to longtime Dallas Cowboys coach Tom Landry.

assoc.t: Tom Landry, longtime Dallas Cowboys coach (surname)
Landry's, restaurant and casino company
Landry Clarke on Friday Night Lights

e.note: One letter away from laundry, which invites teasing.

e.meaning: form of Welsh Merfyn, from words for marrow and eminent
e.etymology: From the Welsh name Merfyn, probably mer, marrow, plus myn, eminent, borne by a 9th-century king of Gwynedd. It reached English as a surname and then a first name.
namesakes: Marvin Harrison (Hall of Fame NFL receiver)

assoc.t: Marvin the Martian of Looney Tunes
Marvin Gaye, Motown soul singer
Marvin windows and doors
Marvin the Paranoid Android (Hitchhiker's Guide)

e.etymology: A phonetic spelling of Tatum, an English surname from a place name meaning Tata's homestead. The YouTube twins Taytum and Oakley Fisher raised its profile.
A pet form of Joe, from Joseph, Hebrew for he will add. For girls it is a short form of Josephine or Joanna.

assoc.t: Joey Tribbiani on Friends
joey, a baby kangaroo

e.etymology: A spelling of Jasmine, the fragrant flower, whose name came through French and Arabic from Persian yasamin. Jazmin follows the Spanish form Jazmín.

assoc.t: Princess Jasmine in Disney's Aladdin (same sound)

e.meaning: from Massy, the estate of Maccius
e.etymology: From a Norman surname based on places called Massy in France, the estate of a man named Maccius. Rowland Macy's department store made the name familiar to Americans.

assoc.t: Macy's department stores and Thanksgiving parade

e.etymology: From Hebrew Uriyah, the Lord is my light. In the Bible Uriah the Hittite is the loyal soldier and husband of Bathsheba whom King David sends to die in battle.

assoc.t: Uriah Heep, the scheming clerk in David Copperfield
Uriah Heep, British hard rock band

e.etymology: From Hebrew aliza, joyful, used as a Hebrew counterpart of the Yiddish name Freyde. In the US it also serves as a spelling of Eliza or Alisa.
A short form of Danielle, Daniela or Daniel, from Hebrew Daniyel, God is my judge. In Spanish and Hungarian it is an everyday nickname for boys named Daniel.
The Greek word for the moon and the name of the moon goddess, sister of the sun god Helios. It is probably related to selas, light or brightness.

assoc.t: Selene, Greek goddess of the moon
Selene, Kate Beckinsale's vampire in Underworld

e.meaning: Galilee, the region of northern Israel
e.etymology: The Spanish and Italian name for Galilee, the region of northern Israel where Jesus preached, from Hebrew galil, district. Mexican TV host Galilea Montijo made it familiar to Spanish-speaking families.
From Hebrew zakkai, pure or innocent. Zaccai appears in the Old Testament, and Yohanan ben Zakkai was a 1st-century sage. In the US it also rides the popularity of Kai and Zachary.
The modern Greek form of Nicholas, from Greek Nikolaos: nike, victory, and laos, people. Saint Nicholas of Myra is the figure behind Santa Claus.
A French name from a pet form of Herleva, a Germanic name whose first part means army. Herleva, also called Arlette, was the mother of William the Conqueror.
The Spanish and Portuguese form of Vincent, from Latin Vincentius, from vincere, to conquer. Saint Vincent of Saragossa is widely venerated in Spain and Portugal.

assoc.t: Vicente Fernández, Mexican ranchera legend

e.meaning: French form of Julian, from Julius; traditionally read as youthful
e.etymology: The French form of Julian, from Latin Julianus, belonging to Julius, the Roman family name of Julius Caesar.

assoc.t: King Julien, the lemur in the Madagascar films

e.etymology: From Hebrew chayyim, life, the same word as in the toast l'chaim, to life. It is a traditional Ashkenazi Jewish name, sometimes added to a sick person's name as a blessing.

assoc.t: Haim, the sister rock band (same word, said HY-im)

e.note: It opens with the throaty kh of Hebrew, which many Americans will say as H or misread as the ch of chair.

e.etymology: From Arabic nur, light. An-Nur, the Light, is one of the names of God in Islam. In Dutch, Noor is separately a short form of Eleonora.
namesakes: Queen Noor of Jordan (American-born queen dowager)

e.etymology: A title in the invented Dothraki language of George R. R. Martin's A Song of Ice and Fire: the wife of a khal, or warlord. The TV series Game of Thrones made it a name through Daenerys Targaryen.

assoc.t: title of Daenerys Targaryen in Game of Thrones

e.note: It is a title, not the character's name, and Daenerys ends the series by burning a city.

e.etymology: From a Hebrew verb meaning to carry or bear a load. Amos was a shepherd from Tekoa whose prophecies form a book of the Old Testament.

assoc.t: Famous Amos chocolate chip cookies
Book of Amos in the Old Testament
Amos 'n' Andy, old radio and TV comedy

e.etymology: As a word, creed means a statement of belief, from Latin credo, I believe. As an English surname it goes back to the Old English personal name Creoda.

assoc.t: Apollo and Adonis Creed of the Rocky and Creed films
Creed, the rock band (Higher, With Arms Wide Open)
Creed Bratton on The Office
Creed fragrances, maker of Aventus
Assassin's Creed video game series

e.etymology: In India, from Sanskrit ila, earth or speech, the name of a figure in Hindu mythology. The vintage American Ila, common around 1900, is of unclear origin; it is also a Hungarian short form of Ilona.
A Hawaiian-style name ending in lani, the Hawaiian word for sky or heaven, which also means royal. It is used alongside Kailani and Leilani.

assoc.t: Kehlani, R&B singer (said the same way)

e.etymology: From Hebrew ya'el, ibex or mountain goat. In the Book of Judges Yael, or Jael, kills the enemy general Sisera. It is a girls' name in Israel; in Latin America and the US it is given mostly to boys.
From Scottish Gaelic Domhnall, from Celtic roots meaning world and rule. It was the name of early Scottish kings and of Clan Donald.

assoc.t: Donald Trump, US president
Donald Duck, Disney cartoon character

e.note: Now strongly tied to President Donald Trump, which many people will read as a political signal.

e.etymology: A pet form of Angela, Angelina and Angelica, all from Greek angelos, messenger or angel.

assoc.t: Angi, formerly Angie's List, home services site
Angie, 1973 Rolling Stones ballad

e.etymology: From an English surname meaning son of Ode, a medieval form of Otto, the Germanic name built on a word for wealth. American use honored the Revolutionary patriot James Otis.
namesakes: Otis Milburn (lead character of Sex Education)

assoc.t: Otis elevators and escalators
Otis Redding, soul singer
Otis Spunkmeyer cookies and muffins

e.etymology: From Gaelic mac, son, the prefix of Scottish and Irish surnames such as MacDonald. It began as a nickname for men with those surnames and is also a short form of Max.

assoc.t: Mac, Apple's line of computers
MAC Cosmetics
mac, short for macaroni, as in mac and cheese
Big Mac, the McDonald's burger

e.etymology: From a Scottish surname taken from a place near Glasgow, Hugh's town. The Texas city is named for Sam Houston, general and president of the Republic of Texas.

assoc.t: Houston, Texas, fourth-largest US city
Whitney Houston, singer (surname)
Houston, we have a problem, the Apollo 13 line

e.meaning: dyer of cloth; also Latin for right-handed, skillful
e.etymology: From an English occupational surname for a dyer, Old English deagestre. It matches the Latin word dexter, right-handed or skillful.

assoc.t: Dexter Morgan, serial-killer antihero of TV's Dexter
Dexter, boy genius of Dexter's Laboratory
Dexter bowling shoes

e.note: Many adults will think first of Dexter Morgan, the serial killer of the TV series Dexter.

e.meaning: sign or verse (Arabic); color or design (Japanese)
e.etymology: Several unrelated names share this form: Arabic aya, a sign or verse of the Quran; Japanese Aya, written with characters such as color or design; and Hebrew Aya, a bird of prey.
